          What’s Different About the Premier League This Season? Five Trends We’ve Spotted in 2026-27
        
      
                          
                      Oct 9, 2026
          
                      Oliver Hopkins / Author, Jakob Abrahamson / Design, Ithiel Piñero / Data Viz
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
We’re just five matchdays into the 2026-27 Premier League season, but some interesting patterns are already beginning to emerge. Here are five league-wide trends we’ve spotted.
OK, ‘gone’ might be an oversimplification. ‘Evaporating’ could be more accurate.

However you put it, the home win percentage in the Premier League is just 36.0% this season, the lowest rate in the competition’s history. It’s even lower than in the COVID-affected 2020-21 campaign, when the majority of matches were played without fans in stadiums.

The fading importance of home advantage is part of a wider trend. As you can see above, four of the six lowest home win rates in Premier League history have come this decade. Of course, teams would still much prefer to play at home than away, but the extent to which doing so provides an advantage appears to be falling.

The answer is that they're broadly becoming draws rather than away wins. There have been 16 draws in the first 50 matches this season, meaning 32.0% of games have finished level. That’s the highest draw percentage of any Premier League season.
Away wins are also fairly prevalent – 32.0% (16/50) is still the seventh-highest on record – but it’s not as notable as the increase in draws.

Matchday 4 of the Premier League was a good demonstration of this pattern. Across the 10 matches, there was just one home win (Leeds’ 4-1 win against Newcastle), while four of the other nine games finished level.
Had Leeds drawn or lost against Newcastle, MD4 would have become just the fourth matchday in Premier League history not to feature a single home win, and the first since September 2000.
One reason why draws are at an all-time high could be because sides are struggling to hold onto leads this season.

A team has scored first in 45 of the 50 Premier League games played so far, but only 29 of those sides have gone on to win. That gives teams scoring first a win rate of just 64.4%, the second-lowest percentage across the last 14 years, and the fourth-lowest in the campaign’s history.

Bournemouth have been the biggest culprits. They’ve dropped seven points in games that they've scored in first already, with Brentford next on six. Overall, the Cherries have dropped nine points from winning positions having taken the lead in four of their five matches but have failed to win any of them.
When Pep Guardiola joined Manchester City in 2016-17, his arrival led to a revolution in how Premier League sides wanted to play.
Goalkeepers increasingly played shorter, teams became more committed to building from the back, and it felt like monopolising possession became an objective in itself.
Many teams, to varying degrees, tried to replicate Guardiola’s tactics.

But as that style became dominant, opponents increasingly adapted to counter it. Winning the ball back and attacking quickly and vertically in transition has become more popular in recent seasons. And it is becoming increasingly effective, too.
There have been 22 matches this season in which a team has enjoyed at least 60% possession. On only eight occasions has that side gone on to win.
That equates to a win rate of just 36.4%, the third lowest in a Premier League season since we have detailed possession data available (from 2005-06).
It follows last season’s record-low rate of 34.1%. Teams are now set up to be more and more successful without the ball.
Another way to measure that shift is through the rise of counter-attacking football.
Fast breaks – defined as a quick counter-attack beginning in the defensive half against an opposition defence that is at least partially unsorted – are an excellent proxy for measuring counters.
